cards.fix_question: Describe how tissue fluid forms from blood plasma in a capillary network.
cards.fix_answer: At the arteriole end of the capillary the hydrostatic pressure of the blood is higher than the opposing pull of water back in (the lower water potential caused by plasma proteins), so there is a net movement of fluid out. Water and small soluble molecules such as oxygen, glucose, amino acids and ions are forced out through gaps in the capillary wall as tissue fluid. Red blood cells and large plasma proteins stay in the capillary.

cards.fix_question: State two differences in composition between blood and tissue fluid and explain one of them.
cards.fix_answer: 1. Blood contains red blood cells; tissue fluid contains none, because the cells are too large to pass through the gaps in the capillary wall. 2. Blood contains a higher concentration of large plasma proteins; tissue fluid contains little or none, because large proteins are mostly kept in the capillary.
cards.conflict: Existing says plasma proteins are absent from tissue fluid; ours says little or none. Ours is right: tissue fluid has a very low, not zero, protein content.

cards.fix_question: Describe how carbon monoxide combines with haemoglobin and explain the effect of this on oxygen transport.
cards.fix_answer: Carbon monoxide binds to the haem groups of haemoglobin to form stable carboxyhaemoglobin. Haemoglobin has a much higher affinity for carbon monoxide (about 200 to 250 times) than for oxygen, so carbon monoxide competes with oxygen and the binding is very hard to reverse. Less haemoglobin is available to form oxyhaemoglobin, so the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood falls.
cards.conflict: Existing says irreversibly; ours says stable compound with higher affinity. Ours is right: the binding is very strong but is not described as irreversible.

cards.fix_question: Describe the role of plasma in the transport of carbon dioxide.
cards.fix_answer: Most carbon dioxide (about 85 per cent) is carried in the plasma as hydrogencarbonate ions, which form inside red blood cells (catalysed by carbonic anhydrase) and diffuse out into the plasma. A small amount (about 5 per cent) is dissolved in the plasma.

cards.fix_question: Explain how the action of the heart is initiated and controlled.
cards.fix_answer: Heart action is myogenic. The sinoatrial node (pacemaker) sends a wave of excitation across the atria, making them contract. The wave reaches the atrioventricular node, which delays it, then it passes down the Purkyne tissue in the septum to the apex and spreads up the ventricle walls so the ventricles contract from the apex upwards.

cards.fix_question: Discuss the biological factors that need to be considered in the prevention and control of cholera.
cards.fix_answer: Cholera is spread by the faecal-oral route when Vibrio cholerae in faeces contaminates water or food, so control must break this route: safe drinking water (boiling or chlorination), sewage treatment so faeces cannot reach water supplies, and handwashing. Infected people need oral rehydration solution to replace the water and salts lost in diarrhoea, and vaccination can protect people at risk.
